newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN, Western powers disagree over currencies.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN, Western powers disagree over currencies.

text.p: Asian and Western nations disagreed Monday over whether the recent plunge in the value of regional currencies was due to rogue speculators or market forces.
The European Union and the Association of South East Asian Nations were also in deep disagreement over whether to extend a European technical cooperation pact to Burma, a new member of ASEAN.

Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad ensured the currency issue would be a major talking point in his keynote address last week to the first of several ASEAN meetings, when he lambasted international currency speculators.
He later named billionaire George Soros as the key figure, saying the American fund manager was punishing ASEAN economies for admitting Burma as a new member.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah continued the attack Monday. "It is really the height of international criminality that the fate of millions could be subject to the mercy of a few unscrupulous traders," he said.
But U.S. Undersecretary of State for Economic and Business Affairs Stuart Eizenstat strongly defended Soros at a closed session of the ministerial conference.

"Experience suggests that market movements are not dominated by a small number of currency speculators, let alone one person, who happens to be a U.S. citizen," he said in a statement later released to the media.
"Blaming these events on speculators is not supported by the evidence," Eizenstat declared.
The United States is one of the largest trading partners and foreign investors in ASEAN, which now groups Brunei, Burma, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
With a total population of 480 million people and combined gross domestic product of $632 billion, the region has become an important economic and political bloc.
ASEAN's dialogue partners are the United States, Russia, China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India and the European Union.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, in a speech to the conference, urged the rapidly developing economies in the region to support a global financial services pact by a Dec. 12 deadline.
"No country can have a world class, high-tech economy without a world-class, properly regulated financial services sector to allocate capital more efficiently," she said.
Malaysia and other countries in the region have been reluctant to open the sector to more foreign investment, saying domestic banks could not survive in global competition.

ASEAN and the European Union were deadlocked over whether to extend a technical cooperation agreement between the two blocs to Burma, which joined ASEAN last week, much to the dismay of Western governments, which wanted to see Rangoon isolated over its human rights and democracy record.
Western nations want ASEAN to step up pressure on Rangoon's military rulers to proceed with constitutional reform, followed by elections.
Albright told the conference that drug traffickers are "now the leading lights in Burma's new market economy and leading figures in its new political order."
